subject: research/partial-participation
professional: a federated / distributed-optimisation researcher (reviewer for ICML, NeurIPS or a stochastic-approximation journal) who knows the FedAvg partial-participation literature and would check first that the stationary-variance formulas are right and that the result is placed against prior work

evidence.correctness: Ran `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 11 tests OK in 1.0 s. Re-ran experiments/run.py and diffed against experiments/results.txt: identical (deterministic seeds). Recomputed independently with a script that does not import the repo (scratchpad indep.py): it iterates the exact second-moment recursion over the Binomial(N,p) law of K, and derives the formula by hand (x'=(1-alpha s)x+alpha*mean noise gives Var = alpha Vw m/(s(2-alpha s)) with skipped rounds cancelling). (1) Rule A, N=6, p=0.3, alpha=0.8, Vw=0.25: 0.102639 against paper 0.10264. (2) Rule B, N=6, p=0.6: 0.0500000 and p=0.3: 0.1250000, against 0.05000 and 0.12500 (the closed form is exact, not just within 0.5%). (3) Matched-speed row N=32, p=0.1, alpha s=0.02: Rule A floor 0.004081 against 0.0041. (4) Rule B mean-square contraction at alpha s=2/c, N=8, p=1/8 evaluates to 1.0000000, so the stated stability edge 2/c is exact. (5) Plain participation-bias fixed point (0,1,2) with p=(0.9,0.5,0.1): 0.46667 against 0.4667. Every number matched. Caveat: the model is a single scalar quadratic mode with Gaussian noise, so correctness is of the formulas for the stated model only.
evidence.completeness: Claimed in README/whitepaper and checked: exact Rule A floor (works, results 1), exact Rule B floor and stability limit 2/(sc) (works, results 1 and 3), matched-speed comparison and small-step limit E[K|K>=1]E[1/K|K>=1] (works, results 4, 1.3389 reproduces), participation bias and inverse-propensity fix with simulation (works, results 5), 11 tests (11 exist, pass), figure experiments/matched_speed.svg exists, live page line present. Limitations section is explicit about what is not done (correlated churn, estimated p_i, Rule A bias under heterogeneity). No stubs or TODOs found. Not done and not claimed: any multi-dimensional or non-quadratic check, any real-trace participation data.
evidence.verification: Test command above: 11 pass. Four hand-seeded mutations in model.py, each reverted with git checkout (git status clean afterwards). M2: inv_mean's weights scaled 1.02 -> caught (2 failures). M4: 1% factor on the Rule B variance -> caught (1 failure). M1: c_factor's (1-p)/(Np) term scaled by 0.9, a 10% error in the factor that drives the headline stability limit 2/(sc), contraction 1-1/c and the Rule B floor -> NOT caught, 11/11 pass. M3: the literal Rule B simulator divides by max(K,1) instead of Np (a different algorithm) -> NOT caught, because the only simulation test uses a 5% tolerance. Causes: the c_factor tests are self-consistent (they compare c_factor with functions built from c_factor, e.g. 1-1/c endpoints), nothing pins c_factor or alpha_max_fixed to a hand number, and test_rule_b_stability_limit contains a vacuous assertion (isinf(x) or x>0). Several tests restate the implementation formula (small-step ratio test recomputes the same algebra). The suite catches gross errors but not a 10% error in the central constant.
evidence.craft: Read model.py (144 lines), tests/test_model.py, experiments/run.py, results.txt, figure.py header. Clean, pure-stdlib, docstring states the derivation, exact binomial sum instead of an approximation, results script reproduces every paper number deterministically. Defects: penalty_avg takes an unused alpha_s argument; test_rule_b_stability_limit has a vacuous assertion and test_rule_a_penalty_is_alpha_free computes an unused-in-effect `full`; inv_mean(N,p) with p<=0 divides by zero or yields 0/0 and no input validation anywhere (N<1, p outside (0,1], eta*a>=1); math.comb with p**k underflow for large N is untreated; the simulator is O(N) per round in a Python loop. Small and honest, nothing copied or silently falling back.
evidence.claims: Checked each README/whitepaper claim against a file. 'matched to simulation within 0.5%': results.txt ratios 0.995 to 1.002, backed (six configurations, one seed each; the unit test only asserts 5%). 'averaging wins only at fast rates': results 4 shows A/B 0.957 at contraction 0.276, backed. 'Np*m = 1.15-1.29 at Np=2-3.2': results 2 rows 1.1531 (Np=2) and 1.2930 (Np=3.2), backed. Stability 1.07/1/s and 0.47 at Np=1: results 3, backed. 0.034 vs 0.22 at N=32,p=0.1: results 4 last line, backed. Bias 0.467 vs 1.000, sim 0.465/0.998 and the 0.011 vs 0.100 two-worker case: results 5, backed. Disclosure present: the paper opens with *Stylised* and states the model and a Limitations section. Weakness: no claim of novelty is made, but the Relevance advice ('divide by the expected cohort, not the realised one') is presented without saying it matches the usual unbiased FedAvg aggregator and without any citation, so a reader cannot tell what is new.
evidence.fitness: A researcher building on this gets a correct, runnable exact-formula kit for one model, which is useful as a baseline or a unit test for a bigger analysis. But the whitepaper cites no external literature at all (grep for fedavg, fednova, federated, arxiv, et al returns nothing; it cites only sibling projects). Nearest prior work a researcher would need named: Li, Huang, Yang, Wang, Zhang, 'On the convergence of FedAvg on non-IID data' (ICLR 2020) and Yang, Fang, Liu 'Achieving linear speedup with partial worker participation' (ICLR 2021), which analyse partial participation with unbiased aggregation; Wang, Liu, Liang, Joshi, Poor 'Tackling the objective inconsistency problem' (FedNova, NeurIPS 2020) and Wang and Ji 'A unified analysis of federated learning with arbitrary client participation' (NeurIPS 2022), which already derive the participation-induced objective bias; Gu et al., MIFA (NeurIPS 2021) and Chen, Horvath, Richtarik 'Optimal client sampling' for propensity-weighting and variance. The inverse-propensity fix is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator and is known. What is plausibly new is the exact stationary variance with E[1/K|K>=1] for participant averaging and the matched-speed A/B crossover; whether that is new is not established because no literature search is shown. No real participation traces, one scalar mode, no target venue named, and it is well below the PhD-programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md (no programme entry, no paper in LaTeX). Usable as a lemma, not yet as a result a researcher can cite.
evidence.domain: A distributed-optimisation reviewer would accept the derivations (checked) and the use of mean-square contraction and a stationary second moment as the right quantities for noisy linear recursions. Departures: (a) independent Bernoulli(p) participation with common p, whereas real participation is correlated with load, price and data (the paper says so); (b) Rule B with the expected count Np is the standard unbiased aggregator, so item 'Relevance' advice is conventional and the interesting novel content is the variance/stability quantification, which is not positioned; (c) the bias analysis in item 4 assumes noise-free quadratics with identical weights w_i and reports the fixed point only, with no variance cost of 1/p_i weights (the IPW stability limit for small p_i is not derived, only listed as untested), so the recommendation 'weight each reporter by 1/p_i' is stated more firmly than the analysis supports; (d) no non-quadratic or multi-mode check, no comparison with an actual FL benchmark. Sound within its stylised model, not the evidence a practitioner would act on.

defects.what: Whitepaper has no citations of external prior work; the nearest literature (FedAvg partial-participation convergence, FedNova, Wang and Ji arbitrary participation, MIFA, Horvitz-Thompson / optimal client sampling) is not named, so novelty of the exact E[1/K|K>=1] floor and of the IPW fix is unestablished

A 10% error in c_factor (the constant driving the Rule B stability limit, contraction and floor) passes all 11 tests, and so does a different Rule B update in the literal simulator (divide by max(K,1) instead of Np); the c_factor tests are self-consistent and the simulation test tolerance is 5%
The 'weight by 1/p_i' recommendation is given without the variance or stability cost of inverse-propensity weights at small p_i; the whitepaper lists estimated p_i as untested
Vacuous assertion `isinf(_f) or _f > 0` in the stability test, and an unused-in-effect `full` variable in the alpha-free test
penalty_avg has an unused alpha_s parameter; no input validation (p<=0, N<1, eta*a>=1 give ZeroDivisionError or garbage)
Single scalar mode, one seed per simulation row, no real participation trace; below the PhD-programme bar in research/CLAUDE.md

verdict: The maths is right: five numbers recomputed by an independent exact-recursion script and a hand derivation all agree with the paper (Rule B floors to 7 digits, the 2/c stability edge exactly), the 11 tests pass, the experiment output reproduces byte for byte, and every number in the README and whitepaper is backed by results.txt with a stylised-model disclosure. It does not meet the bar because verification is a 2: of four hand-seeded mutations two survived, including a 10% error in c_factor, the constant behind the headline stability and contraction results, and the tests partly restate the implementation. Fitness and domain are 2 because the whitepaper cites no external literature at all, although partial participation, objective inconsistency and inverse-propensity weighting are well covered in the federated-learning literature, so a researcher cannot tell what is new; the analysis is for one scalar quadratic mode with Bernoulli participation and no real trace. A sound, finished lemma-level note, not yet a citable result. Cheapest improvements: pin c_factor and alpha_max_fixed to hand-computed values, tighten the simulation tolerance or use a seed-averaged check, add a related-work paragraph with the citations above.
